solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Carp here, perhaps, to discover dreadful shop inside

indicators.note: the jumbled 'shop' goes inside the word meaning 'discover'

parts.note: to discover something is to find it

indicators.note: something dreadful is in a terrible state, so the letters of 'shop' are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written, then shuffled

explanation.surface: An angler grumbling about finding a nasty shop where the carp should be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carp here' reads as a complaint, as in to carp, but carp is the fish and the phrase with 'perhaps' defines by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Carp are commonly kept in garden or ornamental ponds, so this is where such fish might be found.

clue.text: Raid easy to fix, one supposes

indicators.note: the letters of 'raid easy' need fixing, that is rearranging into proper order

parts.note: the eight letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone guessing that a raid will be simple to arrange.
explanation.walkthrough: All eight letters of RAID EASY rearrange into I DARE SAY.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a conversational hedge meaning probably or I suppose, voicing a guess.

clue.text: Artist fine after employee flipped and went on rampage

indicators.note: a flipped word is turned over, so 'employee' is written backwards
the word for 'fine' is placed following the flipped 'employee'

parts.note: RA, Royal Academician, is the usual crossword artist
an employee is a man, as in 'master and man'; here backwards
fine means all right, OK

explanation.surface: An artist, fined after a staff member went berserk, reports a workplace incident.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine' looks like a penalty in the surface but is the adjective OK. 'And' simply joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To run amok is an idiom for behaving wildly and destructively, exactly like going on a rampage.

clue.text: Everything you own's in base condition

parts.note: e is the base of natural logarithms
a condition is a state, as in 'a state of repair'

explanation.surface: A gloomy remark that all your possessions are in poor shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Base' reads as low or shoddy in the surface, but it is the mathematical constant e.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's estate is the total of their property and assets, especially counted at death.

clue.text: Delightful Grand Hotel close to Brindisi — serving porcini, perhaps?

parts.note: delightful, enjoyable: fun
G is the standard abbreviation for grand
Hotel is H in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only the final letter of 'Brindisi' is wanted

parts.note: the final letter of the Italian port

explanation.surface: A glowing review of a smart hotel near Brindisi whose restaurant serves porcini.
explanation.walkthrough: The Italian setting is a disguise: Grand and Hotel are just G and H. Porcini are a kind of mushroom, and the question mark flags a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Porcini are one example of edible mushrooms, which in Italian are called fungi or funghi.

clue.text: Obscure player has expert game

parts.note: to obscure is to blind, as a window blind obscures a view
a player in chess or draughts is a man
has shortened to 's, as in 'she's got'
an expert enthusiast is a buff, as in 'film buff'

explanation.surface: A little-known sportsman turns out to be a master of some pastime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has' contributes just the S of the contraction 's.
explanation.definitionFit: Blind man's buff is a traditional children's party pastime where a blindfolded player tries to catch others.

clue.text: Lowest-level streams flounder?

definitions.note: singular example; the answer is plural

parts.note: the lowest level of anything is its bottom
feeders are tributary streams that feed a river

explanation.surface: The lowest streams struggle and falter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flounder' looks like a verb meaning struggle, but it is the flatfish, an example of the answer, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: The flounder is a flatfish that lives and forages on the seabed, a classic example of fish eating from the floor.

clue.text: Insubordination certain, so fuss made

indicators.note: the letters of 'certain so fuss' are made into something new

parts.note: thirteen letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Disobedience was assured, so a great fuss was kicked up.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole of CERTAIN SO FUSS rearranges into the answer; 'made' is the only signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Fractiousness is unruly, irritable resistance to control, close in sense to rebellious disobedience.

clue.text: Engraver/artist lacking beginnings of skill

indicators.note: the artist goes without the letters that follow, so they are removed from the front

parts.note: a sketcher, with its opening pair taken away

indicators.note: the beginnings of a word are its opening letters, here the first two of 'skill'

parts.note: the two opening letters, which are the ones removed

explanation.surface: An engraver or artist who lacks basic ability.
explanation.walkthrough: The artist is a SKETCHER; drop SK, the first two letters of 'skill'. The slash makes 'artist' look like part of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An etcher cuts designs into metal plates with acid, a kind of printmaking craftsman.

clue.text: Distant destination — one for the visitors

parts.note: distant, far off: away
a destination is an aim or goal

explanation.surface: A far-flung holiday spot recommended to tourists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Visitors' suggests tourists, but in football the visitors are the away team.
explanation.definitionFit: In football an away goal is one scored by the travelling side, the team playing at the opponent's ground.

clue.text: Modelmaker's timber

indicators.note: the possessive says the timber belongs to the word 'Modelmaker', held within its letters

parts.note: found in the middle of the word

explanation.surface: The wood a modelmaker prefers.
explanation.walkthrough: The word sits inside moD-EL-Maker; balsa is the wood that springs to mind, but it is too long.
explanation.definitionFit: Elm is a hardwood tree whose wood is used for furniture, so it counts as a type of lumber.

clue.text: Two numbers by vacuous entertainers may be non-starters

parts.note: No is the abbreviation for number, taken twice

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so 'entertainers' loses its contents and keeps only its two ends

parts.note: just the first and last letters

explanation.surface: Songs by empty-headed performers are likely to flop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Numbers' suggests songs in the surface; here each is just the abbreviation NO.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-no is something forbidden or unacceptable, just as a non-starter is an idea with no chance.

clue.text: The setter (dreadfully iffy about time): 'Could it really be ten to two?'

definitions.text: 'Could it really be ten to two?'

parts.note: the setter refers to himself as I, which is also one

indicators.note: the jumbled 'iffy' goes round the letter for 'time'
something done dreadfully is done badly, so the letters of 'iffy' are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, then shuffled
T is the usual abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: The setter, unsure of the hour, wonders whether it is ten to two.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole question: ten to two on a clock is 1.50, read aloud as one-fifty.
explanation.definitionFit: A digital clock shows ten minutes before two o'clock as 1:50, so the time could be spoken that way.

clue.text: Composer César's half brother?

indicators.note: only half of the composer's surname is kept, the opening three of its six

parts.note: César Franck, the Belgian-French composer; first half of his surname

explanation.surface: Asking whether someone is César Franck's half-sibling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half brother' reads as a relation, but 'half' belongs with the composer's name and 'brother' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Fra is the Italian title given to a monk or friar, meaning a religious brother.

clue.text: Kill time more than once when things don't go so well

definitions.text: when things don't go so well

parts.note: to off someone is slang for killing them
a day is a period of time; more than one makes it plural

explanation.surface: Idling away the hours repeatedly when life is going badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kill time' reads as one idiom meaning to idle, but the setter splits it; 'more than once' simply makes the period plural.
explanation.definitionFit: An off day is a day on which a person performs below their usual standard.

clue.text: Bearing's jammed in chairlift

indicators.note: the answer is wedged tight within the letters of 'chairlift'

parts.note: the letters after the opening CH

explanation.surface: A mechanical bearing has seized up inside a ski lift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bearing' suggests a machine part, but it means a person's manner.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's air is their manner or demeanour, the way they carry themselves.

clue.text: Ruler, white with age, back after conclusions of top church curia

indicators.note: the reversed word is placed following the three end letters
the conclusion of a word is its end, so each of the next three words gives its final letter

parts.note: the final letters of the three words

indicators.note: the word for 'white with age' is written going back, right to left

parts.note: hoar describes hair grey or white from age

explanation.surface: An aged, white-haired ruler returns after the top church court has finished.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a pope and the Vatican curia, but the church words only supply end letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A pharaoh was a king of ancient Egypt, so the title names a kind of monarch.

clue.text: Refuse to budge from last company

parts.note: to last is to hold, as good weather holds
a company is a firm

explanation.surface: Declining to leave the most recent employer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last' reads as an adjective, final, but it is the verb meaning endure.
explanation.definitionFit: To hold firm is an idiom for standing one's ground and not yielding under pressure.

clue.text: Meticulous in dress, old setters welcoming run out

indicators.note: to welcome is to take in, so 'old setters' take in 'run out'

parts.note: a rig is an outfit, as in 'rig-out'
O is the standard abbreviation for old
on cricket scorecards a run-out dismissal is recorded as ro
setters speaking of themselves say us

explanation.surface: A fastidious dresser; old gun dogs let in to escape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setters' could be dogs, but refers to crossword setters as a group, US. 'Run out' is the cricket dismissal, abbreviated on the scorecard.
explanation.definitionFit: Rigorous means extremely thorough and careful, attending precisely to every detail.

clue.text: Ghanaian chanted a sea song

indicators.note: chanted words are spoken or sung, so it is the sound of 'a sea song' that counts

parts.note: a shanty is a sailors' work song

explanation.surface: A man from Ghana sang a sailors' song.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ashanti are a people of central Ghana, once a powerful kingdom.
explanation.definitionFit: Ashanti names both a region of Ghana and its people, so an Ashanti is one kind of Ghanaian.

clue.text: Providers of transport for old crocks?

definitions.text: Providers of transport for old crocks?

parts.words: Providers of transport for old crocks?
parts.note: surface reading: vehicles that carry ailing old people or clapped-out cars
setter's reading: crocks are pieces of crockery, carried on a flat platter at teatime

explanation.surface: Who gives lifts to decrepit old folk or broken-down bangers?
explanation.walkthrough: An old crock is British slang for a frail person or an old car; here it is simply crockery.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea trays are flat carriers used to bring cups, saucers and pots to the table.

clue.text: Cast has Romeo in short hairpiece

indicators.note: the hairpiece is cut short, losing its final letter
the shortened hairpiece has, that is holds, 'Romeo' within it

parts.note: a toupee missing its last letter
Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: The actor playing Romeo wears a skimpy wig.
explanation.walkthrough: The theatrical surface makes 'Romeo' a role, but it is just the letter R.
explanation.definitionFit: A troupe is a company of performers, the same group as a play's cast.

clue.text: Developer of Morning Star

parts.note: am, ante meridiem, marks the morning
a star is a celebrity or idol

explanation.surface: Who founded the Morning Star, a British left-wing daily newspaper?
explanation.walkthrough: The Morning Star is a British socialist newspaper, which makes 'developer' look like its founder; amidol is a photographic chemical.
explanation.definitionFit: Amidol is a chemical agent used in darkrooms to bring out the image on exposed photographic paper.

clue.text: Ear bone irritating at first for 'man of horror'

parts.note: lug is slang for an ear
os is the Latin and anatomical word for bone

indicators.note: only what comes first in 'irritating' is kept, its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: An annoying bone in the ear is a real horror.
explanation.walkthrough: Bela Lugosi was the Hungarian-American actor famous as Dracula in the 1931 film.
explanation.definitionFit: Lugosi was a star of classic horror films, known above all for playing the vampire Count Dracula.

clue.text: Scuttle with husband over foot of pyramid

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for husband
O is over in cricket scoring

indicators.note: the foot of a word is its bottom or end, so only the last letter of 'pyramid' is used

parts.note: the final letter

explanation.surface: Scurrying off with your husband to the base of a pyramid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scuttle' looks like a verb, hurry, but it is the noun: a coal scuttle.
explanation.definitionFit: A hod is a coal scuttle, a metal bucket for carrying coal to the fireplace.

clue.text: Nip out, leaving Minneapolis in conveyance to find pudding

indicators.note: 'Nip' is taken out of the city's name
being conveyed means being moved around, so the remaining letters are carried into new positions

parts.note: the city's name without one N, one I and the P

explanation.surface: Popping out of Minneapolis in a car to pick up dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters N, I and P need not be together in MINNEAPOLIS: remove them wherever they fall and rearrange the remaining eight.
explanation.definitionFit: Semolina is coarse wheat flour, cooked with milk and sugar as a traditional British school dessert.

clue.text: Neglect furnace temperature

parts.note: a forge is a smith's furnace
T is the abbreviation for temperature

explanation.surface: Failing to keep an eye on how hot the boiler is.
explanation.walkthrough: The heating-system picture hides a simple charade.
explanation.definitionFit: To forget to do something is to fail to attend to it, the same as overlooking it.

clue.text: Organisations like AA finance radicals

parts.note: to finance something is to support it with money
in chemistry a radical is a group of atoms acting as a unit

explanation.surface: Bodies like the Automobile Association bankrolling extremists.
explanation.walkthrough: AA suggests the British motoring organisation, but here it is Alcoholics Anonymous. 'Radicals' sounds political but is chemical.
explanation.definitionFit: Alcoholics Anonymous is a well-known example of a mutual-help fellowship where people meet to aid each other's recovery.
